entries.title: Why Cleopatra, Lawrence of Arabia, Ben-Hur & Other Hollywood Classics Still Look So Good
entries.summary: Cleopatra cost Twentieth Century Fox $44 million, by the studio’s own estimate. That may sound like the budget of one of those genre pictures that winds up going straight to streaming, but if we convert those 1963 dollars into current ones, it comes out to $480 million. The most expensive film ever made up to […]
entries.content:
Cleopa­tra cost Twen­ti­eth Cen­tu­ry Fox $44 mil­lion, by the stu­dio’s own esti­mate. That may sound like the bud­get of one of those genre pic­tures that winds up going straight to stream­ing, but if we con­vert those 1963 dol­lars into cur­rent ones, it comes out to $480 mil­lion. The most expen­sive film ever made up to that point, it remained an indus­try sym­bol of near-par­o­d­i­cal­ly trou­bled pro­duc­tion and grotesque cost infla­tion for decades. Like The Wiz­ard of Oz, it failed to recoup its invest­ment dur­ing its ini­tial the­atri­cal run, even­tu­al­ly turn­ing a prof­it thanks only to re-releas­es and tele­vi­sion rights sales. And yet, these six decades lat­er, the invest­ment seems to have proven sound, at least accord­ing to the video above from YouTube chan­nel Wolfcrow, “Why Cleopa­tra Still Looks Like a Tril­lion Bucks.”

Unlike some infa­mous­ly expen­sive movies, Cleopa­tra does­n’t leave you won­der­ing where all the mon­ey went. Wolfcrow cre­ator Sareesh Sud­hakaran points out some of the myr­i­ad ways it man­i­fests onscreen, from the 70-foot-long giant sphinx to the full-scale Alexan­dria har­bor built on the coast to the Roman Forum set designed to be three times larg­er than the actu­al Roman Forum to the 65 or so out­fits Eliz­a­beth Tay­lor wears in the title role (to say noth­ing of the 26,000 oth­er cos­tumes made for all the oth­er char­ac­ters). Even the mat­te paint­ings and opti­cal cam­era tricks still look con­vinc­ing. The film’s pro­duc­tion design­ers knew that noth­ing could be done by half mea­sures, giv­en that the 65mm Todd-AO stock used for film­ing would expose any flim­si­ness on the big screen.

Just as unfor­giv­ing was the ultra-wide aspect ratio used for the 1959 ver­sion of Ben-Hur, which neces­si­tat­ed painstak­ing labor on every­thing that went before the cam­era, but also a new approach to the com­po­si­tion of the shots them­selves. Even those of us who’ve nev­er seen the movie can call to mind images of its cli­mac­tic char­i­ot race, a sequence that earned its cul­tur­al impact the hard way.

It took five months to film on the largest set ever built at that time, with 1,500 extras in its stands. A few years lat­er, Lawrence of Ara­bia took Hol­ly­wood grandeur up to the lev­el of sub­lim­i­ty with its real desert land­scapes. David Lean “was obsessed with scale and detail,” Sud­hakaran explains. “He want­ed the desert to be more than just a back­drop. He want­ed it to be a char­ac­ter in the sto­ry,” which required metic­u­lous plan­ning of all the ways its nat­ur­al light could pos­si­bly be used to dra­mat­ic effect.

Though Sud­hakaran clear­ly has an inter­est in spec­ta­cles from the gold­en age of the Hol­ly­wood his­tor­i­cal epics, he’s also made videos on last­ing­ly impres­sive movies from oth­er times and gen­res. When was the last time you sat down to enjoy the satir­i­cal urban tech­no-dystopia Robo­Cop, the com­ic-strip noir fan­ta­sia of Dick Tra­cy, or the flam­boy­ant de-famil­iar­ized twen­ty-third cen­tu­ry of The Fifth Ele­ment — or bet­ter yet, saw them prop­er­ly screened at a revival house? When they came out, those films met with vary­ing degrees of box-office suc­cess and crit­i­cal praise, if not regard­ed as the absolute peak of cin­e­mat­ic sophis­ti­ca­tion. In our time, their ambi­tion and craft look noth­ing short of aston­ish­ing, espe­cial­ly when we remem­ber that they built their worlds in phys­i­cal real­i­ty with real human beings, most­ly ana­log tech­niques, and a whole lot of labor and imag­i­na­tion. Could even a tril­lion dol­lars buy the same results today?

entries.title: Soviet-Era Illustrations of J. R. R. Tolkien’s The Hobbit (1976)
entries.summary: Until I read J. R. R. Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings, my favorite book growing up was, by far, The Hobbit. Growing up in Russia, however, meant that instead of Tolkien’s English version, my parents read me a Russian translation. To me, the translation easily matched the pace and wonder of Tolkien’s original. Looking […]
entries.content:
Until I read J. R. R. Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings, my favorite book grow­ing up was, by far, The Hob­bit. Grow­ing up in Rus­sia, how­ev­er, meant that instead of Tolkien’s Eng­lish ver­sion, my par­ents read me a Russ­ian trans­la­tion. To me, the trans­la­tion eas­i­ly matched the pace and won­der of Tolkien’s orig­i­nal. Look­ing back, The Hob­bit prob­a­bly made such an indeli­ble impres­sion on me because Tolkien’s tale was alto­geth­er dif­fer­ent than the Russ­ian fairy tales and children’s sto­ries that I had pre­vi­ous­ly been exposed to. There were no child­ish hijinks, no young pro­tag­o­nists, no par­ents to res­cue you when you got into trou­ble. I con­sid­ered it an epic in the truest lit­er­ary sense.

As with many Russ­ian trans­la­tions dur­ing the Cold War, the book came with a com­plete­ly dif­fer­ent set of illus­tra­tions. Mine, I remem­ber regret­ting slight­ly, lacked pic­tures alto­geth­er. A friend’s edi­tion, how­ev­er, was illus­trat­ed in the typ­i­cal Russ­ian style: much more tra­di­tion­al­ly styl­ized than Tolkien’s own draw­ings, they were more angu­lar, friend­lier, almost car­toon­ish. In this post, we include a num­ber of these images from the 1976 print­ing. The cov­er, above, depicts a grin­ning Bil­bo Bag­gins hold­ing a gem. Below, Gan­dalf, an osten­si­bly harm­less soul, pays Bil­bo a vis­it.

Next, we have the three trolls, argu­ing about their var­i­ous eat­ing arrange­ments, with Bil­bo hid­ing to the side.

Here, Gol­lum, né Sméagol, pad­dles his raft in the depths of the moun­tains.

Final­ly, here’s Bil­bo, ful­fill­ing his role as a bur­glar in Smaug’s lair.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2014.

Ilia Blin­d­er­man is a Mon­tre­al-based cul­ture and sci­ence writer.

entries.title: The Names of Nearly 4 Million Enslaved People in Former British Colonies Are Now Searchable Online, Helping Descendants Find Lost Ancestors
entries.summary: A few years ago, we featured here on Open Culture the Freedmen’s Bureau Project database, which contains searchable information on formerly enslaved people in the United States after its Civil War. With nearly 1.8 million men, women, and children registered there when it first opened to the public, it has remained a valuable resource for […]
entries.content:
A few years ago, we fea­tured here on Open Cul­ture the Freedmen’s Bureau Project data­base, which con­tains search­able infor­ma­tion on for­mer­ly enslaved peo­ple in the Unit­ed States after its Civ­il War. With near­ly 1.8 mil­lion men, women, and chil­dren reg­is­tered there when it first opened to the pub­lic, it has remained a valu­able resource for many Amer­i­cans research­ing their own her­itage, not just descen­dants of for­mer slaves but of oth­er Civ­il War refugees as well. But of course, the U.S. was hard­ly the only coun­try where slav­ery exist­ed. Count­less peo­ple here in the twen­ty-first cen­tu­ry have ances­tors who were enslaved in oth­er for­mer British colonies, and now they’ve got a por­tal through which to do genealog­i­cal search­es of their own.

Launched by a part­ner­ship between the geneal­o­gy com­pa­ny Ances­try and the Cen­tre for the Study of the Lega­cies of British Slav­ery at Uni­ver­si­ty Col­lege Lon­don, the online For­mer British Colonies Enslave­ment Reg­is­ters makes avail­able records on near­ly four mil­lion indi­vid­u­als enslaved between 1813 and 1840 in a host of coun­tries from the Bahamas to Mau­ri­tius to South Africa.

First cre­at­ed by the British gov­ern­ment dur­ing the process of abol­ish­ing the transat­lantic slave trade in 1807 — much as the Freedmen’s Bureau orga­nized its reg­istry of for­mer slaves dur­ing Recon­struc­tion under Abra­ham Lin­coln — the orig­i­nal papers con­tain not just their names and ages, but also mater­nal fam­i­ly con­nec­tions, phys­i­cal descrip­tions, and some­times details about their place of African ori­gin.

In the video above, geneal­o­gist and Ances­try Senior Sto­ry Pro­duc­er Nic­ka Sewell-Smith pro­vides an intro­duc­tion to the For­mer British Colonies Enslave­ment Reg­is­ters, which you can access here. If you’re curi­ous about whether your own ances­tors may appear in its records, you can search by details like name, approx­i­mate date, or loca­tion to nar­row down the poten­tial match­es. The mod­ern descen­dants of peo­ple enslaved in the 20 coun­tries cov­ered by the data­base by no means live exclu­sive­ly, or even pri­mar­i­ly, in those coun­tries or in Great Britain itself. More than two cen­turies lat­er, their descen­dants live all over the world, includ­ing in Latin Amer­i­ca and the Unit­ed States, lead­ing lives very dif­fer­ent from those of their enslaved ances­tors — but the recon­struc­tion of their fam­i­ly sto­ries has only just begun. Enter the data­base here.

entries.title: The Bialetti Moka Express: The History of Italy’s Iconic Coffee Maker, and How to Use It the Right Way
entries.summary: I am sure that many an Open Culture reader has a Bialetti Moka Express in their kitchen. I know I do, but I must add that I knew little about its history and apparently even less about how to properly use one. Coffee expert and author of The World Atlas of Coffee James Hoffmann introduces […]
entries.content:
I am sure that many an Open Cul­ture read­er has a Bialet­ti Moka Express in their kitchen. I know I do, but I must add that I knew lit­tle about its his­to­ry and appar­ent­ly even less about how to prop­er­ly use one. Cof­fee expert and author of The World Atlas of Cof­fee James Hoff­mann intro­duces us to the appli­ance we think we know in the above video.

Alfon­so Bialet­ti didn’t orig­i­nal­ly get into the cof­fee busi­ness. In 1919, the Bialet­ti com­pa­ny was an alu­minum man­u­fac­tur­er, with the Moka Express invent­ed some­where around 1933 by Lui­gi de Pon­ti, who worked for the com­pa­ny. Accord­ing to Decon­struct­ing Prod­uct Design by William Lid­well and Ger­ry Man­ac­sa, the inspi­ra­tion came from Bialetti’s wife’s old-fash­ioned wash­ing machine: “a fire, a buck­et, and a lid with a tube com­ing out of it. The buck­et was filled with soapy water, sealed with the lid, and then brought to a boil over the fire, at which point the vapor­ized soapy water was pushed up through the tube and expelled on to the laun­dry.”

As Hoff­mann shows, ear­li­er cof­fee-mak­ers did use steam and a drip tech­nique, but the Moka Express was the first all-in-one mak­er that could sit on the stove top and do the work. All the user had to lis­ten for was the tell-tale gur­gle when it fin­ished brew­ing.

In 1945, Alfonso’s son Rena­to returned from a pris­on­er-of-war camp and took over the fam­i­ly busi­ness. He was instru­men­tal in focus­ing on the Moka Express and turn­ing it into an inter­na­tion­al cof­fee brand. He hired car­toon­ist Paul Cam­pani to design l’omino coi baf­fi, “the mus­ta­chioed lit­tle man” whose image is on the side of every Moka Express, and who, dur­ing the 1950s, was in a series of humor­ous ani­mat­ed com­mer­cials. Bialet­ti was the pride of Italy, and for Ital­ian immi­grants liv­ing abroad, it was a trea­sured object in the kitchen.

Such was the iden­ti­fi­ca­tion of Rena­to Bialet­ti with the Moka Express that when he died in 2016, his ash­es were interred in a giant repli­ca pot. Hoff­mann details the fate of the com­pa­ny after­wards, how it has fared against com­peti­tors in Italy and out­side. Will it still be around in decades? Who knows. But it does make a great cup of cof­fee.

And he shows the cor­rect way to brew a cup with the Moka Express in this oth­er video. Here are a few things I was doing wrong: not using hot water in the bot­tom to start; try­ing to pack in the ground cof­fee like I was mak­ing an espres­so; using too fine a grind; and not cool­ing the bot­tom as soon as it’s done work­ing its mag­ic. (Note: a Moka Express cof­fee is some­where between an espres­so and a pour-over.) All these tips I’m going to try tomor­row morn­ing. Maybe you have been mak­ing your Bialet­ti cup the right way all along. Let me know in the com­ments. I’ll read them over a fresh­ly brewed cup.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2022.

entries.title: The Biggest Ship in History Was Built in China 600 Years Ago—Or Was It?
entries.summary: In 2002, the retired British submarine lieutenant-commander turned amateur historian Gavin Menzies created a stir with a book about Chinese seafaring in the fifteenth century. 1421: The Year China Discovered the World (tellingly titled 1421: The Year China Discovered America in the United States) began as a global history of that year, only coming to focus […]
entries.content:
In 2002, the retired British sub­ma­rine lieu­tenant-com­man­der turned ama­teur his­to­ri­an Gavin Men­zies cre­at­ed a stir with a book about Chi­nese sea­far­ing in the fif­teenth cen­tu­ry. 1421: The Year Chi­na Dis­cov­ered the World (telling­ly titled 1421: The Year Chi­na Dis­cov­ered Amer­i­ca in the Unit­ed States) began as a glob­al his­to­ry of that year, only com­ing to focus on the claim of the title through the inter­ven­tions of pub­lish­ing-indus­try pro­fes­sion­als. They no doubt sensed a lucra­tive con­tro­ver­sy in the off­ing, and events proved them right. Not only did the book turn best­seller, it also man­aged the rare feat of draw­ing, among oth­er respons­es, a two-hour PBS doc­u­men­tary ded­i­cat­ed to debunk­ing it. Today, 1421 is most char­i­ta­bly remem­bered as a work of his­tor­i­cal fic­tion writ­ten around the idea that, even if Chi­na did­n’t actu­al­ly dis­cov­er the world, would­n’t it be neat if it had?

That ques­tion is hard­ly as friv­o­lous as it may sound. Much of Men­zies’ book has to do with the exploits of Zheng He, a Ming-dynasty admi­ral and diplo­mat whose fleet real­ly did make voy­ages to much of the world, or at least the parts sur­round­ing the Indi­an Ocean. Even if the claim that he beat Christo­pher Colum­bus to the Amer­i­c­as can’t be sup­port­ed, he real­ly did get around, and in seri­ous­ly impres­sive ships at that. In the Hoog video above, you can see Zheng He’s sto­ry told with retro 3D video-game graph­ics suit­able to con­vey the kind of adven­ture his life became. Yet it could hard­ly have begun more humbly: born into a Mus­lim fam­i­ly in the south­ern, Mon­gol-con­trolled Yun­nan province, he was cap­tured by the Ming mil­i­tary and cas­trat­ed in ado­les­cence. Harsh though that sounds, it made him able to accrue a kind of pow­er that could nev­er have been his oth­er­wise.

“The Ming empire was built on eunuchs,” says the video’s nar­ra­tor. “Unlike oth­er impe­r­i­al Chi­nese dynas­ties, the Ming ele­vat­ed cas­trat­ed men beyond what any had known.” Their inabil­i­ty to repro­duce and serve their own blood­line inspired the trust of the rulers: “What they lost in muti­la­tion, they gained in access to pow­er.” Under Zhu Di, known as the Yon­gle Emper­or, Zheng He became “the most pow­er­ful eunuch in the Ming Dynasty.” In order to project his pow­er over­seas, the emper­or decid­ed to con­struct “the great­est fleet the world has ever seen,” con­sist­ing of 300 trans­port ships, 180 war­ships, 240 sup­ply ships, 700 horse ships, and 36 mas­sive “trea­sure ships” that might have been the largest wood­en ves­sels ever to set sail. To lead this “mov­ing empire” with its staff of 27,000 — many of them eunuchs — he knew no one more reli­able than his old friend Zheng He.

This fleet’s expe­di­tions main­tained suf­fi­cient hege­mo­ny to ensure a peri­od of region­al sta­bil­i­ty some call the Pax Ming. At the same time, the civ­il ser­vice grew ever more resent­ful of the priv­i­leged eunuch class, and a light­ning strike on the For­bid­den City in 1421 was tak­en as a sign that the time had come to crit­i­cize their lead­er­ship. It would seem that Zhu Gaochi, the Yon­gle Emper­or’s son, took this crit­i­cism to heart. When he took pow­er as the Hongxi Emper­or after his father died while Zheng He was at sea, he put an end to the cost­ly naval expe­di­tions that could, in the­o­ry, one day have reached the New World. Ques­tions about why Chi­na’s age of mar­itime explo­ration had to end have more recent­ly been joined by oth­ers about whether such a vast fleet real­ly could have sailed, and for that mat­ter, whether the enor­mous trea­sure ships could even have been built in the first place. Chi­na may have done away with the eunuch sys­tem more than a cen­tu­ry ago, but there’s no doubt that its cur­rent lead­er­ship rec­og­nizes the impor­tance of sea pow­er — or that it has its eyes on the heav­ens.

entries.title: A 900-Page Pre-Pantone Guide to Color from 1692: A Complete High-Resolution Digital Scan
entries.summary: There’s ahead of its time, then there’s Traité des couleurs servant à la peinture à l’eau — or, in its original Dutch title, Klaer Lightende Spiegel der Verfkonst, a 900-page book of paint colors made before any such things were common tools of the artist’s, scientist’s, and industrial designer’s trade. Author and artist A. Boogert created one, and […]
entries.content:
There’s ahead of its time, then there’s Traité des couleurs ser­vant à la pein­ture à l’eau — or, in its orig­i­nal Dutch title, Klaer Ligh­t­ende Spiegel der Ver­fkon­st, a 900-page book of paint col­ors made before any such things were com­mon tools of the artist’s, scientist’s, and indus­tri­al designer’s trade. Author and artist A. Boogert cre­at­ed one, and only one, copy of his extra­or­di­nary man­u­al on col­or mix­ing in 1692. Appear­ing on the thresh­old of mod­ern col­or the­o­ry, and fea­tur­ing over 700 pages of col­or swatch­es, the book draws on Aristotle’s sys­tem of col­or rather than the new under­stand­ing of the col­or spec­trum, ful­ly elab­o­rat­ed by New­ton in his Opticks over a decade lat­er.

It would be anoth­er hun­dred years before a flood tide of col­or books began to make the the­o­ry more prac­ti­cal: from Goethe’s 1810 The­o­ry of Col­ors and Werner’s 1814 Nomen­cla­ture of Colour to the dream of col­or stan­dard­iza­tion real­ized: the Pan­tone com­pa­ny, launched in 1963.

But if A. Boogert had much influ­ence on the the­o­ry or prac­ti­cal appli­ca­tion of col­or in his day, there doesn’t seem to be much evi­dence for it. Of course most of the Dutch mas­ters had died when the book was com­plet­ed, and it seems unlike­ly that those still work­ing in 1692 would have been famil­iar with its sin­gle copy.

Instead, the book was meant to edu­cate water­col­orists, hence its French title, which refers to “water-based paint.” (A lit­er­al trans­la­tion of the Dutch runs some­thing like “clear­ly light­ing mir­ror of the paint­ing art.”) Medieval his­to­ri­an Erik Kwakkel found the book in a French data­base, “and it turns out to be quite spe­cial,” he writes, “because it pro­vides an unusu­al peek into the work­shop of 17th-cen­tu­ry painters and illus­tra­tors.

In over 700 pages of hand­writ­ten Dutch, the author, who iden­ti­fies him­self as A. Boogert, describes how to make water­colour paints. He explains how to mix the colours and how to change their tone by adding ‘one, two or three por­tions of water.’… In the 17th Cen­tu­ry, an age known as the Gold­en Age of Dutch Paint­ing, this man­u­al would have hit the right spot.”

The book is cur­rent­ly housed at Bib­lio­thèque Méjanes in Aix-en-Provence, where you’ll find full-page, zoomable, hi-res­o­lu­tion scans. “Beyond being infor­ma­tion­al, the images from the book are stun­ning and addic­tive flip through,” notes Refinery29. “They resem­ble page after page of Pan­tone col­or chips, except with­out the house­hold name.” One won­ders if “A. Boogert” would have become a house­hold name had his book been print­ed and dis­trib­uted. But his col­or sys­tem was already pass­ing away in the New­ton­ian age of col­or spec­trums and wheels, until paint chips final­ly came back in style. Vis­it the col­or man­u­al online here.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2019.

Relat­ed Con­tent:

The Vibrant Col­or Wheels Designed by Goethe, New­ton & Oth­er The­o­rists of Col­or (1665–1810)

Josh Jones is a writer and musi­cian based in Durham, NC.

entries.title: David Byrne’s New Book Explores the Strange Afterlife of Good Ideas: From Vermeer’s Paintings to Roman Concrete & Dark Matter
entries.summary: David Byrne will always be most widely known as the co-founder and frontman of Talking Heads. That may count among the greatest possible achievements for any artist — to the minds of many an Open Culture reader, at least — but it must occasionally frustrate the man himself. Talking Heads broke up 35 years ago, […]
entries.content:
David Byrne will always be most wide­ly known as the co-founder and front­man of Talk­ing Heads. That may count among the great­est pos­si­ble achieve­ments for any artist — to the minds of many an Open Cul­ture read­er, at least — but it must occa­sion­al­ly frus­trate the man him­self. Talk­ing Heads broke up 35 years ago, but Byrne has only grown more and more pro­duc­tive since, record­ing his own albums, cre­at­ing musi­cals, writ­ing books, putting on Pow­er­Point pre­sen­ta­tions, and even design­ing bike racks. By now, his ideas have stretched so far beyond music that he’s con­sid­er­ing the nature of ideas them­selves, how they suc­ceed or fail in catch­ing on, and why they go in and out of accep­tance over time. Hence his new book Sleep­ing Beau­ties: Why Good Ideas Go Dor­mant and How They Wake Up.

“I first saw the term ‘sleep­ing beau­ties’ (out­side of the folk­tale or the Dis­ney movie) when I went down a rab­bit hole and stum­bled on a paper from 2004 called “Sleep­ing Beau­ties in Sci­ence” by the sci­en­to­met­rics researcher Antho­ny van Raan at Lei­den Uni­ver­si­ty,” Byrne writes in an excerpt of the book pub­lished online. (Sci­en­to­met­rics being, he adds, “the study of the impact and com­mu­ni­ca­tion of sci­ence.”) He cites a favorite exam­ple of the astronomer Vera Rubin’s dis­cov­ery, in the nine­teen-sev­en­ties, of “evi­dence for dark mat­ter, which is esti­mat­ed to make up a large percent­age of the uni­verse.” Under­stand­ing her own obser­va­tions required her to “ques­tion even her most basic assump­tions — that mat­ter must emit light and radi­a­tion. She was a visu­al thinker, and she used her data to cre­ate plots and sketch­es that revealed pat­terns with­in the num­bers.”

Only decades lat­er was Rubin’s coun­ter­in­tu­itive vision of the uni­verse sup­port­ed by the­o­ret­i­cal physi­cists and radio astrono­mers using ever more tech­no­log­i­cal­ly advanced tools like “the pow­er­ful Hale Tele­scope, Kent Ford’s new spec­tro­graph, and the Uhu­ru satel­lite, which tracked cos­mic X‑rays.” In the Sci­ence Fri­day inter­view at the top of the post, Byrne brings up a much old­er, longer-sleep­ing beau­ty often fea­tured here on Open Cul­ture: ancient Roman con­crete, the source of whose extra­or­di­nary strength and endurance was only deter­mined a few years ago. Though espe­cial­ly vivid in tech­nol­o­gy and sci­ence, “this for­get­ting and then remem­ber­ing, I knew from my own expe­ri­ence, wasn’t lim­it­ed to acad­e­mia,” he writes. “It hap­pens in all kinds of fields and endeav­ors — music, art, lit­er­a­ture, every kind of cre­ative pro­fes­sion.”

As Adam Grant writes in the New York Times Book Review, the range of exam­ples cov­ered in Sleep­ing Beau­ties includes “how advo­cates reawak­ened Bach’s com­po­si­tions and Ver­meer’s paint­ings after one and two cen­turies of slum­ber; how tech­no­log­i­cal advances rekin­dled the­o­ries of con­ti­nen­tal drift and black holes; how acci­dents resus­ci­tat­ed hand-wash­ing and genet­ics; and how war renewed inter­est in the sub­ma­rine and The Great Gats­by.” Mak­ing an appear­ance on Late Night with Seth Mey­ers, Byrne was asked if any of his own work has under­gone a sim­i­lar process of dis­in­ter­est fol­lowed by redis­cov­ery. “It’s kind of the oppo­site,” he replies. “There’s things that I’ve done where I go, ‘That one does not hold up that well at all’ ” — which, if the irony of cul­tur­al his­to­ry con­tin­ues to oper­ate as usu­al, will be exact­ly the records the chil­dren of today’s Talk­ing Heads fans put on most enthu­si­as­ti­cal­ly a few years down the line.

entries.title: The Strange and Brilliant Inventions of Nikola Tesla
entries.summary: Even before the success of the electric car company that now bears his name, Nikola Tesla was a widely respected historical figure. Often, that respect could be based on surprisingly scant knowledge of the man’s life and accomplishments. Didn’t he do something with electricity? Wasn’t he involved in some kind of rivalry with Thomas Edison? […]
entries.content:
Even before the suc­cess of the elec­tric car com­pa­ny that now bears his name, Niko­la Tes­la was a wide­ly respect­ed his­tor­i­cal fig­ure. Often, that respect could be based on sur­pris­ing­ly scant knowl­edge of the man’s life and accom­plish­ments. Did­n’t he do some­thing with elec­tric­i­ty? Was­n’t he involved in some kind of rival­ry with Thomas Edi­son? Would­n’t we all be enjoy­ing wire­less­ly trans­mit­ted pow­er, too cheap to meter, if his noble, soli­tary efforts had­n’t been thwart­ed by the estab­lish­ment? Well, per­haps. What­ev­er dra­mat­ic sat­is­fac­tions we find in Tes­la’s sto­ry, we can only gauge his genius by sur­vey­ing his actu­al inven­tions, four of which are explained in the new Lost in Time video above.

Tes­la lived from 1856 to 1943, a peri­od of such great tech­no­log­i­cal change that, when he demon­strat­ed a radio-con­trolled boat in an ear­ly phase of his career, some of the onlook­ers “were absolute­ly con­vinced that there was a trained mon­key inside the boat, read­ing his hand sig­nals.” The year was 1898, when the very idea of wire­less con­trol had­n’t entered any­one’s mind — but Tes­la already fore­saw a world of “vehi­cles that dri­ve them­selves, machines doing real work from thou­sands of kilo­me­ters away, and air­craft flown from a dis­tance.” He may have been a tad ear­ly to that game, but his inven­tion of the alter­nat­ing cur­rent pow­er sys­tem and the induc­tion motor hap­pened right on time.

At the end of the nine­teenth cen­tu­ry, “the race to get elec­tric­i­ty to every house­hold in Amer­i­ca” was get­ting into gear. Thomas Edis­on’s direct cur­rent (DC) sys­tem tech­ni­cal­ly worked, but would need a very large num­ber of pow­er sta­tions to move pow­er all over the con­ti­nent. Tes­la did his work on AC as a kind of cor­rec­tion to the short­com­ings of DC, draw­ing what his­to­ry remem­bers as a mer­ci­less neg­a­tive-pub­lic­i­ty cam­paign from Edis­on’s side. But none of its often-grue­some stunts meant to asso­ciate Tes­la’s inven­tion with death were a match for the suc­cess of AC’s imple­men­ta­tion in the new pow­er plant at Nia­gara Falls. More than 130 years lat­er, AC has long pow­ered the vast major­i­ty of homes. But if his­to­ry had gone dif­fer­ent­ly, the Tes­la enthu­si­ast can’t resist ask­ing, would your house also be equipped with its own death ray?

In 1934, at one of his annu­al press con­fer­ences, the 78-year-old Tes­la announced that he’d come up with his most impor­tant inven­tion yet, a weapon so pow­er­ful that it could “end all wars.” Called ‘tele­force,’ it would fire beams so con­cen­trat­ed and ener­getic that they could destroy any tar­get instan­ta­neous­ly upon con­tact. When he died in 1943, Tes­la did­n’t even leave suf­fi­cient doc­u­men­ta­tion to tell whether the thing could have worked. He’d made slight­ly more progress on War­den­clyffe Tow­er, meant as a proof of con­cept for his grander vision of turn­ing the Earth into a giant bat­tery, fill­ing it with elec­tric­i­ty into which all human­i­ty could tap at will. Indus­tri­al­ist J. P. Mor­gan had been foot­ing the pro­jec­t’s bill, but cut off fund­ing when it came out that the ever-ambi­tious Tes­la real­ly intend­ed to build much more than what he’d promised, a wire­less com­mu­ni­ca­tion sys­tem — which, at that time, would have seemed like a pret­ty fan­tas­ti­cal notion in itself.

entries.title: 7 Tips from Edgar Allan Poe on How to Write Vivid Stories & Poems
entries.summary: There may be no more a macabrely misogynistic sentence in English literature than Edgar Allan Poe’s contention that “the death… of a beautiful woman” is “unquestionably the most poetical topic in the world.” (His perhaps ironic observation prompted Sylvia Plath to write, over a hundred years later, “The woman is perfected / Her dead / Body […]
entries.content:
There may be no more a macabre­ly misog­y­nis­tic sen­tence in Eng­lish lit­er­a­ture than Edgar Allan Poe’s con­tention that “the death… of a beau­ti­ful woman” is “unques­tion­ably the most poet­i­cal top­ic in the world.” (His per­haps iron­ic obser­va­tion prompt­ed Sylvia Plath to write, over a hun­dred years lat­er, “The woman is per­fect­ed / Her dead / Body wears the smile of accom­plish­ment.”) The sen­tence comes from Poe’s 1846 essay “The Phi­los­o­phy of Com­po­si­tion,” and if this work were only known for its lit­er­ary fetishiza­tion of what Elis­a­beth Bron­fen calls “an aes­thet­i­cal­ly pleas­ing corpse”—marking deep anx­i­eties about both “female sex­u­al­i­ty and decay”—then it would indeed still be of inter­est to fem­i­nists and aca­d­e­mics, though not per­haps to the aver­age read­er.

But Poe has much more to say that does not involve a romance with dead women. The essay deliv­ers on its title’s promise. It is here that we find Poe’s famous the­o­ry of what good lit­er­a­ture is and does, achiev­ing what he calls “uni­ty of effect.” This lit­er­ary “total­i­ty” results from a col­lec­tion of essen­tial ele­ments that the author deems indis­pens­able in “con­struct­ing a sto­ry,” whether in poet­ry or prose, that pro­duces a “vivid effect.”

To illus­trate what he means, Poe walks us through an analy­sis of his own work, “The Raven.” We are to take for grant­ed as read­ers that “The Raven” achieves its desired effect. Poe has no mis­giv­ings about that. But how does it do so? Against com­mon­place ideas that writ­ers “com­pose by a species of fine frenzy—an ecsta­t­ic intu­ition,” Poe has not “the least dif­fi­cul­ty in recall­ing to mind the pro­gres­sive steps of any of my compositions”—steps he con­sid­ers almost “math­e­mat­i­cal.” Nor does he con­sid­er it a “breach of deco­rum” to pull aside the cur­tain and reveal his tricks. Below, in con­densed form, we have list­ed the major points of Poe’s essay, cov­er­ing the ele­ments he con­sid­ers most nec­es­sary to “effec­tive” lit­er­ary com­po­si­tion.

  • Know the end­ing in advance, before you begin writ­ing.

“Noth­ing is more clear,” writes Poe, “than that every plot, worth the name, must be elab­o­rat­ed to its dénoue­ment before any thing be attempt­ed with the pen.” Once writ­ing com­mences, the author must keep the end­ing “con­stant­ly in view” in order to “give a plot its indis­pens­able air of con­se­quence” and inevitabil­i­ty.

  • Keep it short—the “sin­gle sit­ting” rule.

Poe con­tends that “if any lit­er­ary work is too long to be read at one sit­ting, we must be con­tent to dis­pense with the immense­ly impor­tant effect deriv­able from uni­ty of impres­sion.” Force the read­er to take a break, and “the affairs of the world inter­fere” and break the spell. This “lim­it of a sin­gle sit­ting” admits of excep­tions, of course. It must—or the nov­el would be dis­qual­i­fied as lit­er­a­ture. Poe cites Robin­son Cru­soe as one exam­ple of a work of art “demand­ing of no uni­ty.” But the sin­gle sit­ting rule applies to all poems, and for this rea­son, he writes, Milton’s Par­adise Lost fails to achieve a sus­tained effect.

  • Decide on the desired effect.

The author must decide in advance “the choice of impres­sion” he or she wish­es to leave on the read­er. Poe assumes here a tremen­dous amount about the abil­i­ty of authors to manip­u­late read­ers’ emo­tions. He even has the audac­i­ty to claim that the design of the “The Raven” ren­dered the work “uni­ver­sal­ly appre­cia­ble.” It may be so, but per­haps it does not uni­ver­sal­ly inspire an appre­ci­a­tion of Beau­ty that “excites the sen­si­tive soul to tears”—Poe’s desired effect for the poem.

  • Choose the tone of the work.

Poe claims the high­est ground for his work, though it is debat­able whether he was entire­ly seri­ous. As “Beau­ty is the sole legit­i­mate province of the poem” in gen­er­al, and “The Raven” in par­tic­u­lar, “Melan­choly is thus the most legit­i­mate of all poet­i­cal tones.” What­ev­er tone one choos­es, how­ev­er, the tech­nique Poe employs, and rec­om­mends, like­ly applies. It is that of the “refrain”—a repeat­ed “key-note” in word, phrase, or image that sus­tains the mood. In “The Raven,” the word “Nev­er­more” per­forms this func­tion, a word Poe chose for its pho­net­ic as much as for its con­cep­tu­al qual­i­ties.

Poe claims that his choice of the Raven to deliv­er this refrain arose from a desire to rec­on­cile the unthink­ing “monot­o­ny of the exer­cise” with the rea­son­ing capa­bil­i­ties of a human char­ac­ter. He at first con­sid­ered putting the word in the beak of a par­rot, then set­tled on a Raven—“the bird of ill omen”—in keep­ing with the melan­choly tone.

  • Deter­mine the theme and char­ac­ter­i­za­tion of the work.

Here Poe makes his claim about “the death of a beau­ti­ful woman,” and adds, “the lips best suit­ed for such top­ic are those of a bereaved lover.” He choos­es these par­tic­u­lars to rep­re­sent his theme—“the most melan­choly,” Death. Con­trary to the meth­ods of many a writer, Poe moves from the abstract to the con­crete, choos­ing char­ac­ters as mouth­pieces of ideas.

  • Estab­lish the cli­max.

In “The Raven,” Poe says, he “had now to com­bine the two ideas, of a lover lament­ing his deceased mis­tress and a Raven con­tin­u­ous­ly repeat­ing the word ‘Nev­er­more.’” In bring­ing them togeth­er, he com­posed the third-to-last stan­za first, allow­ing it to deter­mine the “rhythm, the metre, and the length and gen­er­al arrange­ment” of the remain­der of the poem. As in the plan­ning stage, Poe rec­om­mends that the writ­ing “have its beginning—at the end.”

  • Deter­mine the set­ting.

Though this aspect of any work seems the obvi­ous place to start, Poe holds it to the end, after he has already decid­ed why he wants to place cer­tain char­ac­ters in place, say­ing cer­tain things. Only when he has clar­i­fied his pur­pose and broad­ly sketched in advance how he intends to achieve it does he decide “to place the lover in his cham­ber… rich­ly fur­nished.” Arriv­ing at these details last does not mean, how­ev­er, that they are after­thoughts, but that they are suggested—or inevitably fol­low from—the work that comes before. In the case of “The Raven,” Poe tells us that in order to car­ry out his lit­er­ary scheme, “a close cir­cum­scrip­tion of space is absolute­ly nec­es­sary to the effect of insu­lat­ed inci­dent.”

Through­out his analy­sis, Poe con­tin­ues to stress—with the high degree of rep­e­ti­tion he favors in all of his writing—that he keeps “orig­i­nal­i­ty always in view.” But orig­i­nal­i­ty, for Poe, is not “a mat­ter, as some sup­pose, of impulse or intu­ition.” Instead, he writes, it “demands in its attain­ment less of inven­tion than nega­tion.” In oth­er words, Poe rec­om­mends that the writer make full use of famil­iar con­ven­tions and forms, but vary, com­bine, and adapt them to suit the pur­pose of the work and make them his or her own.

Though some of Poe’s dis­cus­sion of tech­nique relates specif­i­cal­ly to poet­ry, as his own prose fic­tion tes­ti­fies, these steps can equal­ly apply to the art of the short sto­ry. And though he insists that depic­tions of Beau­ty and Death—or the melan­choly beau­ty of death—mark the high­est of lit­er­ary aims, one could cer­tain­ly adapt his for­mu­la to less obses­sive­ly mor­bid themes as well.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2015.
